label: No Reasonable Suspicion for an Investigative Stop of a Person Not in a Vehicle
motion_heading: The Investigative Stop of {client} Was Not Supported by Reasonable Suspicion

review_conditions.display_note: The officer gave a reason for the stop that isn't on the list. Expect the prosecution to rely on it; this section argues only that reasonable suspicion was lacking, so evaluate that reason before filing.
Police found an outstanding warrant for your client. Expect the prosecution to argue under *Utah v. Strieff* that the warrant attenuates the connection between the stop and the evidence.

sentences.text: A Fourth Amendment seizure occurs when “the officer, by means of physical force or a show of authority, has in some way restrained the liberty of a citizen.”
“[T]he question of whether an investigative stop occurred [hinges on whether] the challenged police conduct would lead a reasonable person to believe that the person was not free to leave.”
A Fourth Amendment seizure occurs when “the officer, by means of physical force or a show of authority, has in some way restrained the liberty of a citizen.”

The Supreme Court has explained that “[e]xamples of circumstances that might indicate a seizure, even where the person did not attempt to leave, would be . . . the display of a weapon by an officer, . . . or the use of language or tone of voice indicating that compliance with the officer’s request might be compelled.”
Reasonable suspicion requires a particularized and objective basis for suspecting the particular person stopped of wrongdoing.
Under the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution, an officer cannot stop a person without reasonable suspicion of criminal activity.

Under *Coleman*, a police officer may only temporarily detain someone for an investigative stop if the officer “has a reasonable suspicion that imminent public danger exists or serious harm to persons or property has recently occurred.”
Once the constitutionality of police action is challenged, the State bears the burden of showing that the officer’s actions were reasonable.
Courts in Alaska use a balancing test to determine whether the officer’s suspicion was reasonable and sufficient for a stop.

sentences.text: Under this balancing test, courts weigh the “degree of threat to public safety and the imminence of that threat” against the “strength of the officer’s reasonable suspicion and intrusiveness of the stop.”
Weighing the “degree” of the public safety threat requires that there be some public safety threat—the officer has to see some evidence of a crime or threat to public safety.
An officer's unparticularized suspicion or hunch is not enough.
Presence in an area of expected criminal activity, standing alone, does not supply reasonable suspicion.
An anonymous tip that lacks indicia of reliability does not, by itself, supply reasonable suspicion.

practice_notes: The stop's lawfulness is judged by what the officer knew before the stop. Facts learned afterward (smell, admissions, contraband) can't justify it retroactively.
If the stop falls, everything that followed (observations, statements, search results) is potentially fruit — consider which later issues depend on it.

The thresholds for suggesting this section were drafted by me and built at the maintainer's request, pending legal review (see the REVIEW CAREFULLY note): no reason given; only weak reasons (high-crime area, nervousness, time of day, furtive movements, something else); an unidentified, uncorroborated tip; a known vehicle or person where the officer had reason to think it was someone else; a general-only description. Flight and an observed crime don't trigger it alone, and count as real reasons.

strieff_attenuation review note (2026-10-12): drafted by Claude. Strieff (2016) as I recall it: discovering a valid, pre-existing arrest warrant after an unlawful stop attenuated the connection to evidence found in the search incident to the arrest. From memory, unverified. The maintainer chose to show the note in both courts for now.
